md:
### Cardiac repairs at a glance

| Injury | Repair |
|---|---|
| Small laceration | Pledgeted 4-0 polypropylene (horizontal mattress, purse-string or running; pledgets of PTFE, felt or autologous pericardium); a stapler works on the low-pressure right heart |
| Wound beside a coronary | Mattress suture passed under the vessel, so it is neither encircled nor kinked |
| Small coronary branch | Tie it |
| Major coronary injury | Close the wound and bypass with vein; no definitive repair without bypass if distal myocardium is threatened |
| Large wound | Pressure or a side-biting clamp until bypass is running |
| Pericardial tear | Close or patch to prevent herniation |
| Impaled object | Leave it until the chest is open |
| Retained foreign body | Remove at the index operation (embolisation, infection, erosion) |

Source: summarised from "Cardiac injury" (TSRA ch. 114) and the AAST and FRCS Atlas additions in this tab.
anchor: Pericardial tears are closed or patched to prevent herniation

md:
### Airway and oesophageal injury side by side

| | Tracheobronchial | Oesophageal |
|---|---|---|
| Where and with what | Blunt tears above the thoracic inlet or within 2 cm of the carina | Over 80% of thoracic cases have another chest injury |
| First step | Secure the airway bronchoscopically into the distal trachea or opposite bronchus | Contrast swallow followed at once by contrast CT |
| Clue or test | Lung that will not re-expand, large continuous leak or stridor: injury until bronchoscopy shows otherwise | Endoscopy: negative predictive value 100%, positive only 33% |
| Access | Cervical: neck incision, intubate a divided trachea directly. Lower: right thoracotomy or clamshell, divide the azygos, intubate across the field | Found late or through the wrong incision: wide drainage, then delayed repair or exclusion with a cervical oesophagostomy |
| Repair | Debride, keep the lateral blood supply, interrupted absorbable sutures without tension, vascularised flap | Two layers over a debrided edge, flap cover |
| Afterwards | Bronchoscopy at one week | Stents not advised in trauma |

Source: summarised from "Airway and oesophagus" (TSRA ch. 115) and "Haemothorax and pneumothorax in trauma" in this tab.
anchor: Stents are not advised in trauma.

md:
### SABR against surgery: the evidence as presented

| Study | Result as presented | Caution |
|---|---|---|
| MISSILE (Louie) | 40% still had viable cancer after SABR | SABR does not treat the lymphatics |
| STARS and ROSEL pooled (Lancet Oncology) | Three-year survival 95% with SABR, 79% with surgery | First author is Chang, not Roth |
| BMJ, SABR against sublobar resection in the elderly | Surgery better | |
| JCO emulated trial (England) | Three-year mortality 30.3% after SABR, 21.6% after surgery; gap about 4% in the over-80s | The over-80s figure is not confirmed; reports say only that the gap narrowed |
| Revised STARS (Chang) | Single-arm SABR compared with VATS lobectomy | Single-arm design |
| Faculty conclusion | First-line for T1–2 N0 M0 is reasonable; for patients fit for either, surgery has the better survival data | NICE and the UK Consortium limit SABR to T1a–T2b, 5 cm or less |

Source: summarised from Case 9 and "Where my notes differ from published sources" in this tab.
anchor: Faculty conclusion: SABR is a good treatment and can be used first-line

md:
### Nodule features: which way they point

| Feature | Points to benign | Points to malignant |
|---|---|---|
| Calcification | Most reliable benign sign, especially uniform; popcorn in hamartoma | Eccentric calcification is less reliable: a cancer can engulf a calcified focus |
| Border | Hamartoma: smooth, lobulated, fat plus soft tissue | Irregular, spiculated or lobulated |
| Growth | Stable for more than 2 years; very rapid growth over days or weeks suggests infection | Growth is the hallmark; mean doubling time of solid cancers 149 days |
| Location | Multiple central nodules along the bronchovascular bundle: sarcoidosis, hypersensitivity pneumonitis | Primary cancers favour the upper lobes, metastases the lower |
| Number | Multiple: infection or scarring | Multiple: metastases, uniform in shape but varied in size |
| Air bronchogram | Airspace filling, more often benign | Seen in adenocarcinoma in situ |
| Ground glass | Non-specific (for example oedema) | May be in situ or minimally invasive adenocarcinoma; needs over 2 years of surveillance |
| PET | Infection or inflammation gives false positives | False negatives under 8 to 10 mm, in situ or minimally invasive and mucinous adenocarcinoma, carcinoid |

Source: summarised from "Work-up of the solitary pulmonary nodule" (TSRA ch. 7) in this tab.
anchor: Investigate if growing, more than 3 cm, or a solid component develops.

md:
### Ventilatory support in contusion and flail chest: the evidence at a glance

| Intervention | Study | Finding |
|---|---|---|
| PEEP | McGee and Trinkle 1972 (animal); Sladen (n = 9, own controls) | Smaller experimental contusions; PEEP 10 or 15 cmH2O improved PO2 in all, dead space unchanged |
| Mode | Pinella: IMV (n = 144) against historical continuous mandatory ventilation | No difference in ventilator duration, PEEP, FiO2 or outcome; no mode proven superior |
| CPAP (animal) | Pigs | 10 to 15 cm CPAP beat IMV alone for alveolar closure, shunt and compliance, more so in PC-FC |
| Mask CPAP | Tanaka (n = 59 FC, Class II, historical controls) | Atelectasis 47% against 95%, pneumonia 27% against 70% (p < 0.01); fewer ventilated |
| CPAP with PCA against intubation | Gunduz RCT (25 per arm) | Survival and nosocomial infection "significantly lower in the CPAP group" (wording as printed) |
| HFOV | Funk (n = 17, retrospective) | Started at peak airway pressure over 30 cm and FiO2 over 60%; better PaO2/FiO2; no comparison with aggressive conventional ventilation |
| Independent lung ventilation | Hurst (n = 8, unilateral PC, no controls) | PaO2 72 to 153 mmHg, shunt 28% to 12.6%; 7 of 8 survived |

Source: summarised from "Ventilation: how" in the EAST 2012 pulmonary contusion and flail chest section of this tab (Simon et al., J Trauma Acute Care Surg 2012).
